about: Plain-language explanations of checks for `sp explain`, `sp status` and `sp digest` (component cli). Read by cli/explanations.py and by the Go implementation (internal/cli/explain), so the text lives here only. Each entry answers what was found, why it matters, how to fix it and how to verify it, in everyday words; keep it generic (no environment, no product names of a particular company). {next_scan} stands for next_scan.
next_scan: The next scheduled scan checks again and marks the finding fixed by itself; `sp run <job>` checks now.

ssh.password_auth_enabled.what: This server lets people log in over SSH with a password.
ssh.password_auth_enabled.why: Passwords can be guessed or stolen. Bots try common passwords against every SSH server on the internet all day; one weak password is enough to get in.
ssh.password_auth_enabled.fix:
1. Make sure your own SSH key works first (log in with it in a second terminal).
2. In /etc/ssh/sshd_config (or a file in sshd_config.d/) set: PasswordAuthentication no and KbdInteractiveAuthentication no.
3. Reload sshd (systemctl reload ssh or sshd). Keep the working session open until a new key login works.

ssh.root_login_password.what: The administrator account (root) can log in over SSH with a password.
ssh.root_login_password.why: root is the one account name every attacker knows; with a password it only takes a guess to own the whole machine.
ssh.root_login_password.fix: Set `PermitRootLogin prohibit-password` (or `no`) in the sshd configuration and reload sshd. Administrators log in as themselves and use sudo.

ssh.x11_forwarding.why: Rarely needed on servers; it widens what a compromised client or server can do to the other side.
ssh.x11_forwarding.fix: Set `X11Forwarding no` in the sshd configuration and reload sshd.

overlay.node_key_expiry_disabled.what: A machine's key for the private overlay network never expires.
overlay.node_key_expiry_disabled.why: If the machine is lost or copied, its access to the private network lasts forever.
overlay.node_key_expiry_disabled.fix: Turn key expiry back on in the overlay network's admin console; for unattended servers, record an exception with an owner and an end date instead.

github.token_broad_scopes.what: A code-host token on this machine can do much more than read code (e.g. delete repositories).
github.token_broad_scopes.why: Anyone or anything that can read this machine's token (a script, a compromised tool) gets all of that power, without an expiry date.
github.token_broad_scopes.fix: Create a fine-grained token limited to the repositories and permissions a job needs, with an expiry; keep the broad one for interactive use only, or remove it.

identity.mfa_disabled.what: An account can log in with only a password: two-factor authentication is off.
identity.mfa_disabled.why: Passwords leak through phishing and reuse; with two-factor on, a stolen password alone is not enough.
identity.mfa_disabled.fix: Turn on two-factor authentication for the account, preferably a passkey or security key; store the recovery codes offline.

identity.org_mfa_not_required.what: The organisation does not require two-factor authentication from its members.
identity.org_mfa_not_required.why: One member without it is the weakest door into every repository they can reach.
identity.org_mfa_not_required.fix: Check who lacks it first (they are removed when you switch it on), then require it in the organisation's security settings.

identity.collaborator_unexpected.what: Someone has access to a repository who is not on the expected list.
identity.collaborator_unexpected.why: Forgotten or unknown collaborators can change code or read private work.
identity.collaborator_unexpected.fix: Confirm with the repository owner; remove the access or add the person to the expected list in the instance config.

identity.credential_expired.what: An expired credential is still configured somewhere.
identity.credential_expired.why: It is clutter that hides which credentials matter.
identity.credential_expired.fix: Remove it, or replace it with a new one if something still needs it.

identity.credential_file_readable.what: A file holding a credential can be read by other users of the machine.
identity.credential_file_readable.why: Any other account or process can copy it and act as you.
identity.credential_file_readable.fix: `chmod 600 <file>`; rotate the credential if others may have read it.

identity.deploy_key_unused.what: A repository deploy key has not been used for months (or never).
identity.deploy_key_unused.why: Unused keys are forgotten keys: nobody notices when one leaks.
identity.deploy_key_unused.fix: Delete it; create a new one when a pipeline needs it again.

identity.fork_pr_approval_weak.what: CI runs code from some outside contributors without anyone approving it first.
identity.fork_pr_approval_weak.why: A pull request from a stranger can run code in your CI, sometimes with access to secrets.
identity.fork_pr_approval_weak.fix: Require approval before workflows run for all outside contributors (repository Actions settings).

identity.overlay_acl_allow_all.what: The private overlay network lets every device reach every other device.
identity.overlay_acl_allow_all.why: One compromised laptop or phone can reach every server.
identity.overlay_acl_allow_all.fix: Replace the default allow-all rule with rules per group or tag (who needs to reach what).

identity.overlay_device_dormant.what: A device on the private overlay network has not been seen for a long time.
identity.overlay_device_dormant.why: Lost or retired devices keep their access until removed.
identity.overlay_device_dormant.fix: Remove the device from the overlay network (add it back if it returns).

identity.ssh_key_age_over_365d.what: An SSH key is more than a year old.
identity.ssh_key_age_over_365d.why: Old keys have been copied to more places and outlived their owners' devices.
identity.ssh_key_age_over_365d.fix: Create a new key, add it where the old one is trusted (servers, code host), then delete the old one.

identity.token_age_over_90d.what: An access token is older than the rotation period.
identity.token_age_over_90d.why: The longer a token lives, the more places it has been copied to.
identity.token_age_over_90d.fix: Issue a new token (with an expiry), switch its users over, revoke the old one.

identity.token_classic_full_repo.what: A token can read and write every private repository of its owner.
identity.token_classic_full_repo.why: Whatever uses the token (a script, a CI job) can change any repository if the token leaks.
identity.token_classic_full_repo.fix: Replace it with a fine-grained token limited to the repositories and permissions it needs, with an expiry.

identity.token_expiring_soon.why: When it expires, whatever uses it stops working (an outage).
identity.token_expiring_soon.fix: Rotate it now and note where it is used.

agent.audit_trail_missing.what: The AI coding assistant left no session records recently.
agent.audit_trail_missing.why: Without them you cannot tell afterwards what the assistant read or ran.
agent.audit_trail_missing.fix: Keep session transcripts on (do not disable or shorten their retention).

agent.memory_secret_suspect.what: An AI assistant's memory file contains something that looks like a password or token.
agent.memory_secret_suspect.why: Memory files are read into every session and may be synced or shared.
agent.memory_secret_suspect.fix: Remove the value (note where the secret lives, not what it is); rotate it if it was real.

agent.no_credential_deny_rules.what: Nothing stops the AI assistant from reading credential files (SSH keys, kubeconfigs, tokens).
agent.no_credential_deny_rules.why: A prompt injected through a file or web page could make it read and leak them.
agent.no_credential_deny_rules.fix: Add deny rules for credential paths (e.g. Read(~/.ssh/**), Read(~/.kube/**)) in the assistant's settings.

sbom.no_packages.what: The platform could not list the software installed on this machine.
sbom.no_packages.why: Without the list, new vulnerabilities in that software cannot be matched to this machine.
sbom.no_packages.fix: Check that the host profile matches the OS and that its package manager is installed.

detection.cluster_not_covered.what: A cluster is not watched for attacks (a detection piece is missing there).
detection.cluster_not_covered.why: An intruder in that cluster would not trigger any alert.
detection.cluster_not_covered.fix: Deploy the missing detection parts (sensor, audit log shipping, rules) to the cluster.

detection.sensor_missing.what: The runtime detection sensor is not running on every node.
detection.sensor_missing.why: Attacks on the nodes without it go unseen.
detection.sensor_missing.fix: Check the sensor's DaemonSet: pods that do not start, nodes it does not tolerate.

detection.source_silent.what: A log source that detections rely on has gone quiet.
detection.source_silent.why: Detections built on it are blind until it sends again; silence looks like safety.
detection.source_silent.fix: Check the log shipper and the source (audit logging on, agent running, credentials valid).

detection.ruler_incomplete.what: Some detection rules are not loaded or fail to evaluate.
detection.ruler_incomplete.why: Those attacks would not be detected.
detection.ruler_incomplete.fix: Reload the rules into the log store's ruler and fix the failing queries.

detection.ruleset_stale.what: The detection rules have not been reviewed for a long time.
detection.ruleset_stale.why: New attack techniques appear constantly; old rules miss them.
detection.ruleset_stale.fix: Compare the rules with their upstream sources, update them, and record the review date.

detection.page_route_missing.what: Urgent detection alerts are recorded but sent to nobody.
detection.page_route_missing.why: An attack would be detected and still nobody would act.
detection.page_route_missing.fix: Route severity=page alerts to a receiver that notifies a person (phone, chat, pager).

detection.backstop_missing.what: The cluster has no detection rules of its own; it relies entirely on the central log store.
detection.backstop_missing.why: If the log store is down, attacks in the cluster go unseen.

detection.drill_overdue.what: Nobody has tested whether detection works (no drill recorded).
detection.drill_overdue.why: Untested detection often turns out not to work when it matters.
detection.drill_overdue.fix: Run a harmless drill in a lab and record how long detection took.

detection.drill_failed.what: The last detection drill was not detected in time.
detection.drill_failed.why: A real attack would likely be missed or noticed too late.
detection.drill_failed.fix: Find the slow or silent stage of the pipeline, fix it, and repeat the drill.

http.unauth_root.what: A web service answers without asking who you are, and the platform cannot tell what it is.
http.unauth_root.why: Unknown services are how forgotten admin pages and test tools end up open to everyone on the network.
http.unauth_root.fix: Find out what runs on that address and port (who owns it?). If it should not be reachable, stop it or firewall it; if it should, put a login in front of it.

http.catch_all_unverified.what: A web application answers every address with the same page, so the platform cannot check its login.
http.catch_all_unverified.why: It may be fine (a single-page app) or it may be open; a person has to look once.
http.catch_all_unverified.fix: Open it in a private browser window: if you can see data without logging in, require a login and turn off open sign-up. If it is fine, record an exception with the reason.

metrics.unauth.what: A /metrics page is readable without a login.
metrics.unauth.why: It tells an attacker software versions and internal names, which helps them pick an exploit.
metrics.unauth.fix: Allow only your monitoring server to reach it (firewall or NetworkPolicy), or put it behind auth.

alertmanager.unauth.what: The alert manager can be used by anyone who can reach it.
alertmanager.unauth.why: Someone could silence your alerts before doing something you would otherwise be paged for.
alertmanager.unauth.fix: Put it behind an authenticating proxy, or reach it only through a port-forward.

prometheus.unauth_read.what: The Prometheus query page and API are open without a login.
prometheus.unauth_read.why: It reveals your whole topology: host names, services, versions.
prometheus.unauth_read.fix: Put an authenticating proxy in front, or restrict who can reach it.

prometheus.unauth_remote_write.what: Anyone who can reach this Prometheus can write metrics into it.
prometheus.unauth_remote_write.why: Fake metrics can hide an incident or trigger false alerts, including the security platform's own.
prometheus.unauth_remote_write.fix: Require authentication (or mTLS) on the remote-write receiver, or allow only known senders.

prometheus.admin_api_unauth.what: The Prometheus admin API is on and open.
prometheus.admin_api_unauth.why: Anyone who reaches it can delete monitoring data.
prometheus.admin_api_unauth.fix: Remove --web.enable-admin-api, or put it behind auth.

ollama.unauth.what: An AI model server accepts requests from anyone.
ollama.unauth.why: Others can use your hardware, download or delete models.
ollama.unauth.fix: Bind it to localhost and put an authenticating proxy in front.

loki.unauth.what: The log store can be read and written without a login.
loki.unauth.why: Logs often contain personal data and tokens; anyone can read them or plant fake log lines.
loki.unauth.fix: Put an authenticating proxy in front (per-tenant auth).

tempo.unauth_read.what: The tracing store can be searched without a login.
tempo.unauth_read.why: Traces show internal requests and sometimes their data.
tempo.unauth_read.fix: Put an authenticating proxy in front.

otlp.unauth_ingest.what: The telemetry intake accepts data from anyone.
otlp.unauth_ingest.why: Fake traces can confuse an investigation.

blackbox.open_probe.what: A probe service can be told to fetch any address.
blackbox.open_probe.why: Attackers can use it to reach machines they cannot reach directly (a relay into your network).
blackbox.open_probe.fix: Allow only the monitoring server to call it.

db.reachable.what: A database port can be reached from outside the machine.
db.reachable.why: Databases are a top target: one weak password or a new vulnerability exposes all the data.
db.reachable.fix: Make the database listen only on localhost or a private network; firewall the port.

smb.reachable.what: Windows file sharing (SMB) can be reached.
smb.reachable.why: SMB has a long history of worms and password attacks.
smb.reachable.fix: Limit it to the local network, turn off guest access, or switch it off.

telnet.open.what: Telnet (an old remote login without encryption) is reachable.
telnet.open.why: Passwords travel in clear text; anyone on the path can read them.
telnet.open.fix: Turn telnet off and use SSH.

patch.security_pending.what: Security updates are waiting to be installed on this machine.
patch.security_pending.why: Published fixes tell attackers exactly what to attack; unpatched machines are the easiest way in.
patch.security_pending.fix: Install the updates (e.g. `sudo apt upgrade`), reboot if asked, and turn on automatic security updates.

patch.pending.what: Software updates are waiting to be installed.
patch.pending.why: Old versions collect known bugs, some of them security bugs.
patch.pending.fix: Install the updates in your next maintenance window.

patch.auto_updates_off.why: Someone has to remember to patch; urgent fixes then wait for that person.
patch.auto_updates_off.fix: Turn on unattended security upgrades (Debian/Ubuntu: unattended-upgrades) or your OS's equivalent.

patch.reboot_required.what: Updates were installed but only take effect after a reboot.
patch.reboot_required.why: Until the reboot, the old (vulnerable) code keeps running.

patch.metadata_stale.what: The machine has not checked for updates for a long time.
patch.metadata_stale.why: It cannot know that security fixes exist.
patch.metadata_stale.fix: Refresh the package lists (e.g. `sudo apt update`) and make sure the regular update job runs.

patch.os_updates_pending.why: See security updates: known bugs stay open.
patch.os_updates_pending.fix: Install the OS updates and restart.

fw.host_firewall_off.why: Every service that listens is reachable by anyone on the network, including ones you forgot.
fw.host_firewall_off.fix: Turn the firewall on with a default-deny rule for incoming connections, then allow what you need.

macos.disk_filevault_off.what: The disk is not encrypted (FileVault is off).
macos.disk_filevault_off.why: A lost or stolen laptop gives away everything on it.
macos.disk_filevault_off.fix: System Settings > Privacy & Security > FileVault: turn it on and keep the recovery key somewhere safe.

macos.fw_app_firewall_off.why: Every app that listens on the network can be reached by others nearby.
macos.fw_app_firewall_off.fix: System Settings > Network > Firewall: turn it on.

macos.fw_stealth_off.what: The Mac answers network probes (stealth mode off).
macos.fw_stealth_off.why: It is easier for others on the same network to discover the machine and its services.
macos.fw_stealth_off.fix: System Settings > Network > Firewall > Options: enable stealth mode.

macos.sip_off.why: Malware can change protected system files.
macos.sip_off.fix: Boot into recovery mode and run `csrutil enable`.

macos.gatekeeper_off.what: Gatekeeper (the check that apps are signed) is off.
macos.gatekeeper_off.why: Unsigned, possibly malicious apps run without warning.

patch.brew_outdated.what: Command-line packages installed with Homebrew are out of date.

patch.android_security_patch_old.what: The Android security patch level is old.
patch.android_security_patch_old.why: Phones are full of credentials; old patch levels have public exploits.
patch.android_security_patch_old.fix: Install the system update, or plan to replace a device that no longer gets updates.

patch.windows_stale.what: Windows has not installed updates for a long time.

win.av_realtime_off.fix: Windows Security > Virus & threat protection: turn real-time protection on.

win.av_signatures_stale.what: Malware definitions are out of date.
win.av_signatures_stale.fix: Update the definitions (Windows Security > check for updates).

win.smb1_enabled.what: The old SMB1 file-sharing protocol is on.
win.smb1_enabled.why: SMB1 is what the WannaCry worm used.
win.smb1_enabled.fix: Turn off 'SMB 1.0/CIFS File Sharing Support' in Windows features.

win.disk_unencrypted.what: The disk is not encrypted (BitLocker off).
win.disk_unencrypted.why: A lost or stolen device gives away everything on it.
win.disk_unencrypted.fix: Turn on BitLocker and store the recovery key safely.

telnet.daemon_running.fix: Stop and remove the telnet server; use SSH.

secret.in_process_argv.what: A password or token is visible in a running program's command line.
secret.in_process_argv.why: Every user on the machine can read command lines (e.g. with `ps`).
secret.in_process_argv.fix: Pass the secret through a file with restricted permissions or an environment variable, then rotate it.

repo.default_branch_unprotected.what: Anyone with write access can push straight to the repository's main branch, without review.
repo.default_branch_unprotected.why: One stolen account or one mistake changes production code with nobody looking; force-pushes can erase history.
repo.default_branch_unprotected.fix: Add a branch protection rule (or ruleset) for the default branch: no direct pushes, changes through pull requests with at least one approval and passing checks, no force-push or deletion.

repo.protection_no_approvals.what: The main branch is protected, but a change can be merged without anyone approving it.
repo.protection_no_approvals.why: Review is the control that catches mistakes and malicious changes; without it protection is thin.
repo.protection_no_approvals.fix: Require at least one approving review in the branch protection rule.

repo.deploy_key_write.what: A deploy key can push to the repository.
repo.deploy_key_write.why: Deploy keys often sit on build machines; whoever gets the key can change your code.
repo.deploy_key_write.fix: Make it read-only unless a pipeline really needs to push; rotate it at least yearly.

repo.mirror_unverified_remote.what: A mirror pulls code over plain http.
repo.mirror_unverified_remote.why: Anyone on the path can change the code on its way in.

repo.actions_default_write.what: CI jobs get a token that can write to the repository by default.
repo.actions_default_write.why: A compromised build step (e.g. a bad dependency) can change code or releases.
repo.actions_default_write.fix: Set the default CI token permission to read-only and grant write only to the jobs that need it.

repo.actions_can_approve_prs.what: CI jobs may approve pull requests.
repo.actions_can_approve_prs.why: An automated job could approve its own change, skipping review.
repo.actions_can_approve_prs.fix: Turn off 'allow actions to create and approve pull requests' unless you rely on it.

repo.dependabot_alerts_off.what: Alerts for vulnerable dependencies are off.
repo.dependabot_alerts_off.why: You will not hear about known holes in libraries you use.
repo.dependabot_alerts_off.fix: Turn on dependency alerts and security updates.

repo.dependabot_alerts_open.what: Libraries used by this repository have known serious vulnerabilities.
repo.dependabot_alerts_open.why: Attackers scan for exactly these versions.
repo.dependabot_alerts_open.fix: Merge the proposed security updates (or update the libraries yourself) and release.

repo.secret_scanning_off.what: Secret scanning is off for a public repository.
repo.secret_scanning_off.why: Leaked passwords and keys go unnoticed.

repo.push_protection_off.what: Pushing a secret into the repository is not blocked.
repo.push_protection_off.why: A leaked key is public the moment it is pushed.
repo.push_protection_off.fix: Turn on push protection for secrets.

repo.secret_scanning_alerts_open.what: Secrets (passwords, keys, tokens) were found in the repository.
repo.secret_scanning_alerts_open.why: Treat them as known to attackers: deleting the file does not help, history keeps them.
repo.secret_scanning_alerts_open.fix: 1. Revoke or rotate each secret at its issuer. 2. Then close the alert. 3. Optionally clean history.

vuln.high_fixable_aggregate.what: A running image contains several high-severity vulnerabilities that already have fixes.
vuln.high_fixable_aggregate.why: Known, fixable vulnerabilities are the cheapest way in for an attacker.
vuln.high_fixable_aggregate.fix: Rebuild the image on an updated base image / dependencies and redeploy.

secret.permissions_too_open.what: A file with a secret in it can be read by other users.
secret.permissions_too_open.why: Any other account or process on the machine can copy it.
secret.permissions_too_open.fix: `chmod 600 <file>` (only the owner can read it); rotate the secret if others may have read it.

secret.ssh_key_no_passphrase.what: An SSH private key has no passphrase.
secret.ssh_key_no_passphrase.why: Whoever copies the file can use it immediately, everywhere the key is trusted.
secret.ssh_key_no_passphrase.fix: Add a passphrase (`ssh-keygen -p -f <key>`) and use an agent, or use a hardware key.

secret.kubeconfig_embedded_client_key.what: A Kubernetes config file contains a long-lived client key.
secret.kubeconfig_embedded_client_key.why: The file alone grants cluster access until the certificate expires, often for a year or more.
secret.kubeconfig_embedded_client_key.fix: Use short-lived credentials (OIDC login or `kubectl create token`), or at least limit the identity's rights.

secret.tf_state_plaintext.what: Infrastructure state files are stored unencrypted.
secret.tf_state_plaintext.why: State files usually contain every password the infrastructure uses.
secret.tf_state_plaintext.fix: Move the state to an encrypted backend (or encrypt it at rest) and restrict who can read it.

secret.rclone_config_plaintext.what: A sync tool's configuration stores credentials unencrypted.
secret.rclone_config_plaintext.why: The file alone gives access to the storage.
secret.rclone_config_plaintext.fix: Encrypt the configuration (rclone config password) and restrict the file to its owner.

secret.docker_inline_auth.what: Container registry passwords are stored inline in the Docker config.
secret.docker_inline_auth.why: The file alone gives registry access.
secret.docker_inline_auth.fix: Use a credential helper (OS keychain) instead and log in again.

secret.gh_token_in_file.what: A code-host token is stored in a plain file.
secret.gh_token_in_file.why: Anything that can read the file can act as you.
secret.gh_token_in_file.fix: Store it in the OS keychain (e.g. `gh auth login` uses it) and rotate the token.

secret.credential_in_notes.what: A password or token appears in notes or memory files.
secret.credential_in_notes.why: Notes get shared, synced and read by tools (including AI assistants).
secret.credential_in_notes.fix: Remove it from the notes, keep it in a password manager, and rotate it.

secret.age_over_90d.what: A credential has not been changed for more than 90 days.
secret.age_over_90d.why: The longer a secret lives, the more places it has been copied to.
secret.age_over_90d.fix: Rotate it (issue a new one, switch users over, revoke the old one); automate rotation where possible.

k8s.netpol.missing.what: Pods in this namespace can talk to anything, and anything can talk to them.
k8s.netpol.missing.why: One compromised pod can reach every other service in the cluster.
k8s.netpol.missing.fix: Add a default-deny NetworkPolicy to the namespace, then allow only the traffic each app needs.

k8s.operator_cred_system_masters.what: The credential used to inspect this cluster is a full administrator.
k8s.operator_cred_system_masters.why: If the file leaks, the whole cluster is lost; a read-only check needs no admin rights.
k8s.operator_cred_system_masters.fix: Create a read-only identity for the platform (deploy/kubernetes RBAC) and use that kubeconfig.

k8s.policy.engine_missing.what: The cluster has no admission policy engine.
k8s.policy.engine_missing.why: Nothing stops a risky workload (privileged, host access) from being deployed.
k8s.policy.engine_missing.fix: Install a policy engine (e.g. Kyverno or Gatekeeper) with the baseline Pod Security rules, in audit mode first.

agent.bypass_permissions_default.what: An AI coding assistant runs commands without asking first, by default.
agent.bypass_permissions_default.why: A prompt injected through a file or web page can make it run anything on this machine.
agent.bypass_permissions_default.fix: Set the default mode to ask for permission; allow-list only safe commands.

agent.reads_outside_workdir.what: An AI coding assistant may read files outside the project it works on.
agent.reads_outside_workdir.why: It can read keys, tokens and other projects' data, and might send them somewhere.
agent.reads_outside_workdir.fix: Restrict reads to the working directory (and explicitly listed extra directories).

agent.settings_writable_by_others.what: An AI assistant's settings file can be changed by other users.
agent.settings_writable_by_others.why: Others could grant it more power.

cloud.firewall_admin_port_open.what: A cloud firewall rule (security group, VPC firewall, network security group) lets anyone on the internet reach remote-administration ports (SSH 22, RDP 3389).
cloud.firewall_admin_port_open.why: Bots scan every cloud address for these ports within minutes; one weak password or unpatched service and the machine is taken over.
cloud.firewall_admin_port_open.fix:
1. Change the rule's source from 'anywhere' (the all-addresses range, IPv4 and IPv6) to your office/VPN addresses.
2. Better: remove the rule and use the provider's session service (SSM Session Manager, IAP, Bastion).

cloud.firewall_open_to_internet.what: A cloud firewall rule opens all ports to the whole internet.
cloud.firewall_open_to_internet.why: Every service on the machine, including ones never meant to be public, becomes reachable by anyone.
cloud.firewall_open_to_internet.fix: Replace the rule with rules for the specific ports the service needs, from the sources that need them.

cloud.public_endpoint.what: A cloud resource (instance, database) has a public address.
cloud.public_endpoint.why: It can be attacked directly from the internet, bypassing load balancers and filters.
cloud.public_endpoint.fix: Remove the public address; reach it through a load balancer, a private endpoint or a VPN.

cloud.volume_unencrypted.what: A disk (block volume) or disk snapshot in the cloud is not encrypted.
cloud.volume_unencrypted.why: Copies of the disk (snapshots shared by mistake, a leaked backup) expose all the data on it.
cloud.volume_unencrypted.fix: Turn on 'encrypt new volumes by default' for the account/region; copy data to an encrypted volume and delete the old one.

cloud.instance_unpatched.what: A cloud machine is missing updates, or nothing manages its updates.
cloud.instance_unpatched.why: Known vulnerabilities are exploited within days of publication.
cloud.instance_unpatched.fix: Enrol the machine in the provider's patch management (Systems Manager, OS Config, Update Manager) and apply the missing updates.

cloud.instance_metadata_v1.what: A cloud machine answers metadata requests without a session token (IMDSv1).
cloud.instance_metadata_v1.why: A request-forgery bug in any app on the machine can then steal the machine's cloud credentials.
cloud.instance_metadata_v1.fix: Set the instance's metadata option to 'tokens required' (IMDSv2).

cloud.user_without_mfa.what: A person can sign in to the cloud console with a password but without a second factor.
cloud.user_without_mfa.why: A phished or reused password is then enough to control cloud resources.
cloud.user_without_mfa.fix: Turn on MFA for the user (a passkey or security key is best) and enforce MFA by policy; better, move people to single sign-on.

cloud.root_mfa_disabled.what: The cloud account's root (owner) login has no second factor.
cloud.root_mfa_disabled.why: Root can do everything, including closing the account; its password alone protects it.
cloud.root_mfa_disabled.fix: Add a hardware key or passkey MFA to the root login and store the recovery details offline.

cloud.root_access_key.what: The cloud account's root login has programmatic access keys.
cloud.root_access_key.why: A leaked root key gives full, unrestricted control of the account.
cloud.root_access_key.fix: Delete the root access keys; use roles for automation.

cloud.root_used.what: The cloud account's root login was used recently.
cloud.root_used.why: Day-to-day use of the all-powerful login multiplies the chance of it being stolen.
cloud.root_used.fix: Use named, least-privilege identities; keep root for break-glass only.

cloud.access_key_old.what: A long-lived cloud access key (or service-account key) has not been changed for more than 90 days.
cloud.access_key_old.why: Old keys end up in laptops, logs and repositories; the longer a key lives the likelier it has leaked.
cloud.access_key_old.fix: Replace the key with federation or a role; if a key is unavoidable, create a new one, switch over, then delete the old one.

cloud.credential_unused.what: A cloud password or access key has not been used for weeks.
cloud.credential_unused.why: Nobody notices if an unused credential is stolen and starts being used.
cloud.credential_unused.fix: Disable it, wait a little, then delete it.

cloud.service_account_key_user_managed.what: A cloud service account has a downloadable (long-lived) key.
cloud.service_account_key_user_managed.why: Key files get copied around and leak; whoever has the file is that service account.
cloud.service_account_key_user_managed.fix: Use workload identity federation or the platform's attached service account instead; delete the keys.

cloud.admin_privileges_broad.what: A workload identity holds an administrator role.
cloud.admin_privileges_broad.why: Any bug in that workload becomes full control of the project or account.
cloud.admin_privileges_broad.fix: Grant only the specific roles the workload needs.

cloud.password_policy_weak.what: The cloud account's password policy is weaker than the benchmark (short passwords, reuse allowed).
cloud.password_policy_weak.why: Weak or reused passwords are guessed or come from other sites' leaks.
cloud.password_policy_weak.fix: Require at least 14 characters and prevent reuse; better, move people to single sign-on.

cloud.platform_credential_over_privilege.what: The cloud identity this security platform uses can change things, but it only needs to read.
cloud.platform_credential_over_privilege.why: The platform's credential is a target: if it is stolen it should not be able to change or delete anything. The platform refuses to scan with it until it is fixed.
cloud.platform_credential_over_privilege.fix: Remove every policy/role from the platform's identity except the read-only audit ones (AWS SecurityAudit + ViewOnlyAccess, GCP Security Reviewer + Viewer, Azure Reader + Security Reader; docs/cloud.md).

cloud.storage_public.what: A cloud storage bucket or container can be read (or written) by anyone on the internet.
cloud.storage_public.why: Public buckets are found by automated scanners; their contents leak or get replaced.
cloud.storage_public.fix: Turn on 'block public access' for the account and the bucket; share single files with signed URLs or through a CDN with origin access.

cloud.storage_unencrypted.what: A cloud storage bucket has no default encryption setting.
cloud.storage_unencrypted.why: New objects may be stored unencrypted, against most policies and benchmarks.
cloud.storage_unencrypted.fix: Enable default encryption (provider-managed or your own key) on the bucket.

cloud.storage_insecure_transport.what: A cloud storage bucket accepts plain-HTTP requests.
cloud.storage_insecure_transport.why: Data and credentials could be read or changed on the network.
cloud.storage_insecure_transport.fix: Add a policy that denies requests without TLS (AWS: aws:SecureTransport false; Azure: secure transfer required).

cloud.snapshot_public.what: A disk snapshot or machine image is shared with everyone.
cloud.snapshot_public.why: Anyone can copy the disk and read the data or secrets on it.
cloud.snapshot_public.fix: Remove the public sharing permission; block public sharing at account level.

cloud.audit_log_disabled.what: The cloud account does not record who did what (audit trail missing or off in some regions).
cloud.audit_log_disabled.why: Without it an intrusion cannot be detected or investigated.
cloud.audit_log_disabled.fix: Create an account-wide, all-regions audit trail (CloudTrail, Cloud Audit Logs, Activity Log export) into protected storage.

families.what: A container runs in privileged mode: it has almost the same power as the machine (node) itself.
families.why: If that container is broken into, the attacker owns the node and usually the cluster.
families.fix: Remove `privileged: true` from the pod spec. If the workload needs one specific power, grant only that capability; run it as non-root.

families.what: A pod mounts a directory of the node.
families.why: It can read or change node files (often credentials).
families.fix: Use a normal volume; if a node path is needed, mount it read-only and as narrow as possible.

families.what: A pod shares the node's own processes, network or IPC.
families.why: It can see or reach things on the node that ordinary pods cannot.
families.fix: Remove hostPID / hostNetwork / hostIPC unless the workload is a node agent that truly needs it.

families.what: A container is given extra Linux powers (capabilities).
families.why: They make escaping the container easier.
families.fix: Drop all capabilities and add back only the one the app needs.

families.what: A pod is configured with more power than ordinary workloads need.
families.why: Extra power turns a small break-in into a big one.
families.fix: Follow the remediation line below; compare with the Kubernetes Pod Security 'restricted' profile.

families.what: An account in the cluster has broad rights (admin, wildcard or secret-reading).
families.why: Whoever controls that account (or its token) controls much of the cluster.
families.fix: Give the account a role with just the verbs and resources it needs; remove cluster-admin bindings that are not for people doing break-glass work.

families.what: A workload breaks one of the cluster's own admission policies.
families.why: The policy describes something your team decided is unsafe.
families.fix: Change the workload to satisfy the policy, or record an exception with an owner and an end date.

families.what: The cluster fails an item of the CIS Kubernetes benchmark (a public hardening checklist).
families.why: Each item closes a known way to attack or misuse a cluster.
families.fix: Read the benchmark item's remediation text (in the finding) and apply it on the node or control plane.

families.what: A cloud security check (CIS Foundations benchmark or a scanner's best practice) failed for this resource.
families.why: Each check closes a known way to attack or leak data from a cloud account.
families.fix: Read the remediation line and the engine's reference (refs) below; apply it in the account, or record an exception with an owner and an end date.

families.what: A known vulnerability (CVE) affects software you run.
families.why: Public vulnerabilities, especially ones listed as exploited in the wild (KEV), are attacked at scale.
families.fix: Update the affected package or image to a fixed version and redeploy. If none exists, reduce exposure (no public access) and record an exception with an end date.

families.what: An AI coding assistant is allowed to run a broad class of commands without asking.
families.why: Broad rules (any shell, any network tool) let an injected prompt do real damage.
families.fix: Replace the broad rule with specific, read-only commands.

families.what: A vendor published a security advisory that may concern a product you run; a person has to check it.
families.why: Vendor advisories are often not in machine-readable databases; the platform only knows it mentions you.
families.fix: Read the advisory, decide whether you are affected, update if so, and record the decision.

families.what: A phone or tablet is missing a monthly Android security update.
families.why: The missing update fixes known flaws, some of them exploited in the wild.
families.fix: Install the system update; plan to replace devices that no longer receive updates.

families.what: An Apple device is missing a security update.
families.why: It fixes known flaws, some of them exploited in the wild.
families.fix: Install the update (Settings > General > Software Update) and restart.

families.what: A Windows machine is missing a monthly security update.
families.why: It fixes known flaws, some exploited in the wild.
families.fix: Run Windows Update and restart.

families.what: A database listens on every network interface of this machine.
families.why: It can be reached from the network, not only from the apps on this machine.
families.fix: Make it listen on localhost (or a private interface) only; firewall the port.

families.what: A Windows firewall profile is off.
families.why: Services on the machine are reachable from that network type.
families.fix: Windows Security > Firewall & network protection: turn the profile back on.

families.what: A built-in macOS protection is off.
families.why: The Mac is easier to attack or to read when lost.
families.fix: Turn the protection back on in System Settings > Privacy & Security.

families.what: The machine's firewall is not configured to block unexpected incoming connections.
families.why: Forgotten services become reachable.
families.fix: Turn on the firewall with default-deny for incoming traffic.

families.what: The machine is missing updates.
families.why: Known bugs stay open.
families.fix: Install the updates and reboot if needed.

families.what: A secret (password, key, token) is stored in a risky way.
families.why: It can be copied and misused.
families.fix: Restrict the file, move the secret to a secrets manager or keychain, and rotate it.

families.what: A Windows protection is off or out of date.
families.why: Windows machines are the most attacked endpoints.
families.fix: Turn the protection back on (Windows Security) and update it.

layers.identity: who can log in or act, and with which keys
layers.network: what can be reached from the network
layers.supply-chain: where your code and software come from
layers.ai-agents: AI assistants and what they may do
layers.detection: whether an attack would be noticed

severities.critical: fix today: attackers are likely to use this soon
